title: Back to School Night Is Not About Your Syllabus
author: Jennifer Haber
summary: Jennifer Haber, drawing on thirty years of teaching and her own experience as a parent sitting in the audience at Back to School Night, argues that teachers consistently misunderstand what the event is for. She frames the core mismatch precisely: teachers feel responsible for explaining grading policies, homework expectations, and classroom procedures, while parents in the room are actually trying to answer a different question entirely — 'who is the person my child is going to spend the next ten months with?' Her five concrete recommendations follow directly from that reframe: stop reading the packet aloud since parents can access that information later, make even the least exciting parts of the curriculum sound purposeful by explaining the reasoning behind them, rehearse enthusiasm out loud beforehand since 'enthusiasm is not the same as performance' but does require deliberate practice, and greet parents individually as they arrive rather than waiting behind the desk. Haber's clearest marker of success is a specific compliment she's received: a parent telling her 'I wish I could take your class,' which she reads not as praise for her syllabus but as evidence the parent left believing their child is fortunate to have her as a teacher. The essay closes by explicitly stating the reframe as its thesis: after thirty years, she has concluded the evening 'is not really about explaining my classroom. It is about introducing myself.'
points: Haber's reframed question — teachers explain policy while parents are actually asking 'who is the person my child is going to spend the next ten months with?' — identifies a specific, correctable mismatch between what teachers prepare and what the audience is actually listening for.

Her instruction to give a reason for even the 'least exciting part of your curriculum' rather than rushing past it or apologizing for it turns a routine logistics briefing into an opportunity to model the same enthusiasm-for-purpose teachers want students to feel about coursework.

The practice of physically greeting each parent by name and child before the formal presentation begins, rather than waiting behind the desk, operationalizes the essay's thesis into a concrete two-minute-per-parent habit any teacher can adopt immediately.
quotes: As teachers, we feel responsible for explaining everything. As parents, we are trying to answer a different question. Who is the person my child is going to spend the next ten months with?
The greatest compliment I ever receive after Back to School Night is when a parent tells me, "I wish I could take your class.
Whatever the least exciting part of your curriculum is, don't rush past it or apologize for it. Give parents the reason behind it.
If most of those minutes are spent reading through grading categories, attendance policies, classroom rules, and supply lists, parents leave knowing more about our paperwork than they do about us.
This is exactly why the presentation deserves practice, and I mean actual practice, out loud, before the night arrives.
After thirty years of Back to School Nights, I don't think the evening is really about explaining my classroom. It is about introducing myself.
